note: He passes the two commercial criteria on their face and fails both starting-point criteria. Successful is comfortable: a retired-and-rehired school counsellor who is also a working football and basketball official, a track coach with USATF certifications, collecting pensions alongside a full salary. Income passes as stated — 'my income supersedes most retirees, it's well over six figures' — and that is exactly what makes this call diagnostically valuable, because he then disclosed zero dollars available today and a single $400 credit line reserved for emergencies. The criterion tests earnings and this deal was blocked by liquidity, which reinforces the existing observation that 'makes good money' is doing work a payment plan already solves; here even the payment plan failed and only a $200 bridge tier kept it alive. Neglected health is a miss, and arguably backwards: he is the most health-attentive prospect in the batch, with a chiropractor, a podiatrist, annual stress tests, a rowing machine and a sauna blanket, and he has managed 25 years of diabetes without complications. Health is his most-attended area, not his neglected one, and there is a chronic disease in play rather than an absence of attention. Good to great is also a miss — at 69, 224 lb with a 42-inch waist, his own framing is preservation: 'I don't want to lose what I have' and 'I want to get to 78 standing and walking.' That is holding ground against decline, not converting good into great. He does clear the exclusion: active, running on the field as an official, and belonging to multiple gyms. Worth flagging for the wider analysis that the stated ICP has nothing to say about age or chronic disease, and this prospect is 69, turning 70, and diabetic.
